newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk opposition submits censure against government.
newsitem.headline: Turk opposition submits censure against government.

text.p: Turkey's opposition parties on Friday submitted a censure motion against the government in a bid to topple the Islamist-led alliance, a senior opposition MP told reporters.
"The motion has been submitted to the parliament speaker," said deputy Cumhur Ersumer, of the main opposition Motherland Party (ANAP).

The motion, accusing Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and his cabinet of dividing the officially secular country along Moslem-secularist lines, carried the signatures of four of the five opposition parties in parliament.
"The present government, as well as increasing the problems of the country to an unprecedented degree, has dragged our people into fratricidal fighting," the motion said.

Opposition and dissident government MPs have been negotiating for some time to try to bring down the government, which has been attacked by Turkey's traditional elite, particularly the powerful military, for putting the country's secularist make-up in danger.
The motion would need the support of government MPs to bring down the coalition.
Erbakan and his deputy, conservative leader Tansu Ciller, made no immediate comment, but they had both earlier dismissed the attempt to bring them down.
"Do you think anything is going to come from this censure motion? Oh dear, you are going to be let down again, you are going to be disappointed again," Ciller told reporters earlier on Friday.

The government has faced three censure motions since its inception last June, but they have all failed due to a lack of cooperation by the squabbling opposition and less-than-expected support from within Ciller's True Path Party (DYP).
Erbakan has been criticised for seeking deeper ties with Islamist countries and proposing mild reforms of some of Turkey's strict secularist laws.
The government has most recently been split over an education plan -- demanded by the military -- that Erbakan's Islamists fear will hurt Moslem religious schools.
The cabinet has not met for weeks and analysts and the opposition put this down to disputes over the education plan.

The censure motion criticises the government over the education row, as well as economic failures -- a $1 billion budget deficit in first quarter 1997 despite a balanced budget target -- and verbal attacks on the media, which the press have blamed for recent assaults on a television station and a paper.

It accuses the coalition parties of working illegally to cover up corruption and other charges against government members and also criticises its foreign policy, which it says has alienated foreign investors.

"We ask for the censure of the prime minister and the cabinet...who have lost the trust of both our people and MPs who stand by their oath by deepening our country's problems in all areas, adding new problems, constantly breaching the fundamental principles of our republic and bringing our people to the brink of conflict," the censure motion concluded.
